item_taken.first_six_words: Arm's-length custody: a fact about an
item_taken.why: The case is framed, opened and closed, as an arrangement (the State Health Register under Rule 14) that the filing hospital can read but not edit or delete, so that the definition's source is readable rather than inferred, which is custody by who may delete and not Deputized injury (standing exists, the patients simply sign it away), Silence priced as guilt (no rule scores a gap as the worst reading), Trigger's blind spot (the register's not holding purpose is a feature of the case, not its frame), or Room for strangers (the docket exists and is kept empty rather than being a setting that must be built).

reasoning: The fence rule splits on how the tenant-class mechanism in the case is read. The case does not present the State Patient Complaint Docket hearing as a setting that must be built so strangers can compare private memories; the docket already exists. It presents the hearing as the only setting in which two returning patients could learn they returned for the same cause, and then states the mechanism that keeps it from convening: because the share is the registered indicator, the department telephones every counted patient, offers a fee waiver, and obtains a release that includes not filing with the docket, 214 releases signed, no complaint filed, no hearing convened between January 2018 and June 2025. That is the preemption reading, so the rule places the case on the target's side as Unassembled witness. The rule says only that this mechanism changes seat; the register custody, the lost project board, the purposeless filing, and Okafor's review are carried across unchanged because the rule says nothing about them, and they fit the target's stated domain (a witness prevented from forming, a prepared-for alternative that did not occur) without needing restatement.
case_out: A witness that never assembled: a hearing of the State Patient Complaint Docket is the only setting in which two patients of Alder Regional Hospital's emergency department who returned within 72 hours of discharge could learn that they returned for the same cause, since each patient knows only their own return, and no such hearing has convened between January 2018 and June 2025, because since January 2018 the department has telephoned every patient counted in its 72-hour re-presentation share within a week of the return, offered a waiver of the second visit's fee, and asked for a signed release that includes not filing with the docket; 214 releases were signed and no docket complaint concerning a 72-hour return has been filed. The department does this because the share is its registered quality indicator. The share, patients who return within 72 hours of discharge divided by patients discharged that month, was defined in 2017 by the Triage Selection Committee, three clinicians, as the one outcome on which Protocol Q, a five-level triage, and Protocol P, a two-stream fast-track, were predicted to differ; Q was adopted. The committee worked in a hosted project board holding P's proposal, the predictions, and the argument; the board was decommissioned in March 2020 without export, and no copy of P's proposal exists anywhere else. On 3 November 2017 the quality officer, Rhea Lindqvist, filed the share's definition with the State Health Register under Rule 14 as the department's quality indicator; the register is kept by the state, readable by hospitals but not editable or deletable by them, every entry carrying the filing hospital, the date, and the filing officer's name, and it was built to hold the definition, the hospital, the date, and the officer, and not the purpose. The filing carries no statement of purpose, and neither the register nor anything at the hospital names Protocol P. The filed definition is, word for word, the text now in the department's dashboard configuration. Since January 2018 the hospital has filed the share monthly, and the register publishes only the monthly figure, naming nobody. No member of the 2017 committee remains, and Lindqvist left in 2019. In August 2025 the current quality manager, Dana Okafor, who joined in 2023, preparing the annual indicator review, reads the definition in the dashboard configuration and in the register, finds them identical and the filing signed by Lindqvist on 3 November 2017, so the definition's source is readable from the arrangement and not inferred, finds nothing at the hospital or in the register saying why this outcome and not another is the indicator, and drafts the review with the share listed as 'legacy indicator, purpose not recorded, recommend retire'.
